title: Loop-of-Henle countercurrent helium concentrator for fab exhaust
idea: The kidney's countercurrent multiplier concentrates solutes from dilute flows through cascaded exchange. Countercurrent cascades of helium-selective membranes pull dilute helium from wafer-cooling, leak-check and purge exhausts and re-concentrate it to 5N purity for reuse on site.
why: Cuts fab helium purchases 80-95%, neutralizing the Qatar helium chokepoint.

title: Airbnb for stranded server DRAM across a CXL fabric
idea: Modeled on Airbnb renting empty rooms, every server in a hall exposes its unallocated DRAM pages to a CXL switch; a broker lists free capacity, tenants rent GB-minutes, and hardware page-ownership tags plus memory encryption keep tenants isolated while the host can evict with notice.
why: Data-center DRAM is typically 40-60% allocated but idle; renting the stranded half raises effective fleet supply 20-30% without new chips.

title: Airbus-style multinational DRAM fab consortium with offtake shares
idea: Mid-size sovereign users (India, EU states, Canada, Gulf states) each lack scale. A treaty consortium funds one shared fab with offtake rights pro rata to equity, as Airbus and CERN do, sited away from the helium, tungsten and EUV chokepoints.
why: Splits $15B+ capital across 5-8 states and adds a new independent supplier.

title: Negabytes: pay customers to release memory during shortages
idea: Reverse supply and demand, as electricity demand-response does: clouds and memory makers auction credits per GB-month that customers give up through compression, tiering or shorter model contexts. They resell the freed capacity during shortage periods.
why: Usable supply at zero capex: trimming 5-15% of demand in a tight market moves prices more than the same amount of new fab capacity.

title: VLSI Research Association Redux: U.S. Cooperative for EUV-Free DRAM
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where five rivals shared one joint lab and built the steppers and e-beam tools that won DRAM: a time-boxed U.S. cooperative of a memory maker, tool vendors, hyperscalers and national labs co-develops patent-pooled DUV/nanoimprint DRAM process modules, then disbands so members compete on products.
why: Capital and litho: shares the ~$5B R&D for a non-EUV DRAM flow; Japan's version helped move its DRAM share to a majority within a decade.

title: Ship lightly tested dies; in-system BIST finishes the screening
idea: Space parts get exhaustive ATE screening; invert the extreme. Commodity dies get only a short gross test at the fab, and an on-die BIST engine plus host firmware runs the long retention and pattern screens during the customer's first weeks of burn-in, reporting results to the fab's yield database.
why: ATE hours are a capex and throughput bottleneck; halving test time frees tester capacity and cuts ~3-5% from cost per bit.

title: Capacitive-deionization loops regenerate rinse water with reusable carbon electrodes
idea: Rinse effluent flows between charged porous-carbon electrodes whose electric double layers adsorb ions; reversing the voltage releases a small brine stream and regenerates the electrodes, returning low-TDS water to UPW polishing with no chemical regenerants.
why: Reclaims >85% of dilute rinse water at low energy, opening water-capped sites.

title: Farmer's grain co-op: OEMs jointly own a take-or-pay DRAM fab
idea: Thinking like a Midwest grain cooperative, mid-size OEMs (PC, auto, telecom, tier-2 cloud) form a member-owned memory co-op that signs 7-year take-or-pay offtake for a 40k-wafer/month fab and pledges those contracts as collateral for project-finance debt. Members get bits at cost-plus with patronage dividends instead of paying spot prices.
why: Capital intensity and price volatility: turns $15B of equity risk into contract-backed debt at a cost of capital ~2-3 points lower, makes a new U.S. fab bankable, and shields members from 4x price spikes.

title: Substitute leading-edge capacity for legacy DRAM with converted 200mm fabs
idea: Swap making DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 for industrial, auto and defense parts on leading-edge lines for re-tooled shuttered U.S. 200mm fabs running 3x-nm DRAM with depreciated DUV tools.
why: Frees ~10-15% of leading-edge wafer starts for AI-era parts and builds a U.S. DRAM workforce base at <$1B per site.

title: Another dimension: 16-high stacks of depreciated legacy-node DRAM dies
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: keep fully depreciated 2x/1x nm fabs running and gain density vertically by thinning their dies and stacking 16-high with low-cost hybrid or staggered wire-bond packaging for capacity-tier modules.
why: Cost per bit: depreciated wafers are ~40-50% cheaper; stacking restores density without EUV.

title: Dandelion franchise micro-fabs running a 25-mask capacitorless flow
idea: Dandelions spread identical seeds widely. Dropping the capacitor removes the high-AR etch, capacitor high-k stack and support lattice; the remaining ~25-mask flow ships as a turnkey containerized micro-fab kit franchised to regional operators who pay royalties and share a parts depot.
why: Micro-fab capital of ~$0.3-1B vs $15B; distributed U.S. production.

title: Magnify compute, minify state: seed-and-regenerate memory
idea: Store compact seeds (RNG states, layer inputs, low-rank latents) instead of large tensors and regenerate data on demand with spare FLOPs (activation recompute, learned decompression, KV recompute from prefix), with a runtime deciding per tensor whether to store or regenerate.
why: Compute is far more abundant per dollar than DRAM; for training activations and KV caches the stored footprint shrinks ~10-100x, an effective ~100x cut in DRAM $ per job.

title: Wood-frog cryogenic gain cells: mature fabs at 77 K
idea: Wood frogs freeze solid and resume life on thawing. Capacitorless gain-cell memory runs at 77 K in LN2-immersed AI racks, where subthreshold leakage falls by orders of magnitude and retention reaches hours, so older-node fabs can make effectively refresh-free memory.
why: Removes refresh (16-33% of idle power) and lets 65-28 nm fabs compete; cooling cost is partly offset.

title: Substitute DRAM-only supply with an open IP pool for foundry memory tiers
idea: Swap memory vendors' monopoly for a licensing pool that gives every logic foundry a qualified recipe for 4-8 tiers of oxide gain-cell memory built in BEOL at <=400 C above their logic.
why: Turns all U.S. logic capacity into memory capacity without new front-end tools, attacking U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity at once.

title: U.S. back-end memory hubs that import wafers and export modules
idea: Ideal: memory made where it is used. Closest achievable: because the front end holds the capex, put HBM stacking, test, burn-in and module assembly in U.S. packaging hubs that import processed DRAM wafers, and keep onshore wafer inventory.
why: U.S. manufacturability and resilience: 25-35% of value onshore in ~18 months, versus 5 years for a fab.

title: Dry exhaust abatement: sorbent beds instead of water scrubbers
idea: Reverse the scrubber: burn-wet and wet scrubbers on etch/CVD exhaust are replaced by plasma or thermal destruction followed by dry chemisorbent beds (Ca/Al oxides that capture F and Cl). The beds are regenerated or recycled off-site.
why: Exhaust scrubbing draws water nonstop. Dry abatement cuts scrubber water ~10x and recovers fluorine as CaF2 feedstock.

title: Advance market commitment for next-generation memory bits
idea: Combine the vaccine Advance Market Commitment model with memory. Governments and hyperscalers pre-commit to buy the first 10 EB of any DRAM-class technology that meets $/GB, latency and endurance thresholds, at a guaranteed premium price that tapers.
why: Removes the demand-risk valley of death for 3D DRAM, gain-cell or capacitorless entrants. That pulls new tech and new fabs forward by years.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordline using all-TiN fill at sub-10 nm widths
idea: Below ~10 nm width, electron surface and grain-boundary scattering raise W's effective resistivity toward ~30-40 uOhm-cm while its barrier eats the cross-section; mean-free-path math shows a barrierless TiN or Ti-Al-N full fill lands within ~1.5x. Qualify a W-free buried wordline with all-TiN fill and a thin n+ poly-Si cap for work-function tuning.
why: Scarce resource: removes China-sourced tungsten (~80%) from DRAM's most W-intensive layer, at a small RC penalty offset by shorter wordline segments.

title: Capacity-market retainers for DRAM lines that can swing from HBM
idea: Ideal: memory capacity that moves instantly to wherever the shortage is. Closest achievable: as in electricity capacity markets, the government pays a per-wafer-start retainer to keep lines qualified for both HBM and DDR/LPDDR and to switch within 60 days when called during commodity shortages.
why: AI crowding of commodity DRAM: a fast surge lever that avoids 4x price spikes.

title: Sell bits during a node's immature yield ramp
idea: Inverts 'a new node ships only after defect density matures': with up to 1% cell faults absorbed by controller codes, vendors sell error-tolerant parts from the first months of a ramp instead of waiting 12-18 months for near-zero-defect yields.
why: Time to capacity: pulls 6-12 months of saleable output forward on each node and pays down ramp costs sooner.

title: Exchange-traded multi-year DRAM futures that pre-fund fab construction
idea: Inverts 'DRAM is sold spot or by quarterly contract': list standardized 1-5 year bit futures (Gb-equivalent, DDR5 delivery) so new fabs can pre-sell output and post hedged revenue as collateral for construction loans.
why: Capital intensity: lowers cost of capital by several points and breaks the boom-bust underinvestment cycle that produced the 4x spike.

title: Ship untested die; deep test and soft repair at first boot
idea: Inverts 'every die is fully tested before leaving the fab': skip most hours-long wafer-level retention and burn-in testing; the host controller runs deep BIST at first boot, programs soft row remaps, and uploads results to the vendor's yield database.
why: Capital and capacity: memory test is ~10-15% of cost and a throughput bottleneck; frees testers and cuts weeks from cycle time.

title: Depot-level single-chip repair for failed DIMMs
idea: Military depots repair boards rather than replacing them; data centers scrap a DIMM when one of its 18-36 chips fails. A 10-person depot uses X-ray, IR rework and an inventory of harvested chips to replace the single failed package, retest and return the module.
why: Recovers ~95% of each failed module's bits; a large share of RMA'd DIMMs become supply again.

title: Eliminate wafer-reject destruction: rescue dies with tiny remap controller
idea: Eliminate crushing of ink-dotted DRAM dies: buy reject and downgrade wafers at scrap price, characterize dies on rented probers, and pair each with a small address-remap controller in a system-in-package for embedded buyers; $1M covers prober time, OSAT lots and controller design.
why: Recovers bits otherwise destroyed (a few percent of output) for buyers who value availability over density.

title: Tool vendors paid per good wafer, not per tool
idea: Reverse the capex flow: litho, etch and deposition vendors install tools in a new DRAM fab with no upfront charge and are paid a fee per good wafer pass, like aircraft-engine 'power by the hour'. Vendors share yield risk and keep the tools upgraded.
why: Capital intensity: ~70% of fab capex moves off the entrant's balance sheet, so a $15B+ barrier becomes an operating cost that scales with output.

title: Data-lifetime-matched retention grade: short capacitors for AI working memory
idea: Retention only has to exceed the data's lifetime, and AI activations and KV-cache are rewritten every ~1-10 ms, not held for 64 ms. Define a JEDEC short-retention grade with a 4 ms guarantee; since required charge scales with leakage x hold time, Cs can drop ~40% (with shorter bitlines to keep Cs/Cbl), allowing AR ~30-35:1 capacitors built with fewer high-aspect-ratio etch and deposition steps.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital: halving cylinder height removes the hardest HAR steps, lifts yield and frees etch-tool capacity; ~15-25% lower cost per bit for the AI tier.

title: Laundromat: pay-per-wafer-pass tool leasing inside memory fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'laundromat' -> pay per load, never own the washer. Litho, etch and deposition vendors own and maintain tools inside the fab and bill per wafer-pass; they can redeploy tools across fabs as cycles shift.
why: Cuts the memory maker's upfront capex ~40-60%, moves depreciation risk to whoever can redeploy tools, and lowers the entry bar for new DRAM entrants.

title: Pit crew: hot-swap process chamber modules refurbished off-site
idea: Random stimulus 'F1 pit crew' -> swap the tire, fix it later. Etch and deposition chambers become kinematic-mount cartridges; at preventive maintenance a pre-seasoned spare cartridge is swapped in in about an hour while the used one is cleaned at a regional depot.
why: PM downtime falls from ~8-24 h to ~1 h, tool availability rises ~5-8%, and existing fabs ship ~5% more wafers with no new building.

title: Pay-per-wafer-pass equipment leasing from toolmakers
idea: Po: the toolmaker owns the fab. DUV scanner, etch and deposition OEMs keep ownership of their tools inside the DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass with uptime guarantees; the operator carries only building, people and materials.
why: Moves depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) off the entrant's balance sheet and ties OEM revenue to yield and uptime; cuts the entry ticket for a 20k-wafer fab by billions; attacks capital intensity.

title: Closed-loop helium recapture and hydrogen-argon backside cooling
idea: Worse: vent all fab helium and rely on Qatar. Flip: capture helium from wafer backside cooling, leak checking and chamber purges with cryogenic and membrane recovery for >90% recycle, and switch backside cooling in etch and deposition to H2/Ar blends where conductivity suffices.
why: Cuts per-wafer helium demand ~80-90%, removing the Qatar chokepoint from DRAM output.

title: Compliant nano-pillar chuck that cools wafers without helium backside gas
idea: Scale shift from gas conduction to solid contact: the electrostatic chuck surface carries a forest of compliant metal-coated nano-pillars that conform to the wafer's backside roughness and conduct heat directly, replacing helium backside gas in etch and deposition tools.
why: Helium backside cooling is a major fab helium use. A gas-free thermal contact removes it and also ends helium leak-related wafer loss.

title: H: Electrolytic hydrogen replaces helium as electrostatic-chuck backside gas
idea: Use on-site PEM-electrolyzed H2 (thermal conductivity 0.18 vs 0.15 W/mK for He) as the low-pressure backside cooling gas in etch and deposition chucks, with leak sensing and dilution exhaust, and deuterium blends where plasma chemistry requires.
why: Eliminates the largest helium use in DRAM fabs using only water and electricity, available anywhere.

title: Autophagy firmware: servers digest bad DRAM regions, keep the rest
idea: Cells digest damaged organelles rather than dying. Server firmware and OS retire failing rows, banks or chips at fine granularity (page offlining plus rank and chip sparing) and keep using the healthy remainder, instead of replacing whole DIMMs at the first spike of correctable errors.
why: Could halve DIMM replacement rates, extending fleet life and freeing replacement supply.

title: Fleet-wide field post-package repair extends DIMM life
idea: Box[Transform=OS/BMC-triggered soft and hard PPR on correctable-error rows x Integration=standard DDR5 PPR commands x Owner=hyperscaler fleet software]: instead of replacing DIMMs with rising correctable errors, fleet software maps failing rows to spares with JEDEC PPR.
why: Lowers DIMM replacement demand by an estimated 30-50%, extending service life 1.5-2x with the interface unchanged.

title: Open-source eDRAM macro compiler for 22/28 nm foundries
idea: Box[Medium=MIM/trench eDRAM x Access=logic FET x Sensing=open sense-amp IP x Fab=mature foundry node x Owner=open consortium x Finance=membership dues]: publish a silicon-proven, permissively licensed eDRAM macro generator (array, refresh controller, sense amps, BIST) so any 22/28 nm foundry customer can build on-die working memory without buying discrete DRAM.
why: Moves some DRAM demand onto abundant mature-node logic capacity, which has ~3x more global wafer starts than DRAM; cuts discrete-DRAM demand for edge and accelerator SRAM-adjacent buffers.

title: Substitute proprietary cell IP with an open DRAM PDK for mature foundries
idea: Swap closed DRAM cell know-how for OpenDRAM: a government-funded open-source eDRAM/gain-cell library, sense amps and compilers qualified on mature U.S. foundry nodes (90-22 nm), so any foundry can sell memory.
why: Attacks U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share) by turning existing logic fabs into memory suppliers for embedded and edge demand, freeing commodity DRAM for servers.

title: Eliminate the IDM: fabless DRAM tolled on mature logic foundries
idea: Eliminate the integrated DRAM manufacturer: a fabless house designs logic-compatible high-retention DRAM (MIM-capacitor 1T1C or capacitorless) for 22-40nm logic processes and buys wafers from under-utilized foundries, the way fabless modem makers did.
why: Taps the ~20-30% idle mature-node foundry capacity, including US sites, for embedded/industrial DRAM without a $15B fab.

title: Porous materials: anodized macroporous capacitors in legacy 200 mm fabs
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: one mask opens a lattice of seeds and electrochemical anodization grows deep macropores (AR >100:1) for storage capacitors, letting legacy fabs without advanced high-AR plasma etchers produce DRAM.
why: Tool chokepoint and capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches high AR with a wet bath instead of a $10M+ etcher.

title: Skull-melting crystal pullers: silicon held by its own frozen shell
idea: Ideal: a crucible that is never consumed. Closest achievable: cold-wall induction skull melting, where a water-cooled segmented copper cage keeps a frozen silicon shell that holds the melt, replaces the quartz crucible in Czochralski growth, with magnetic fields to stabilize the melt.
why: High-purity quartz chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): eliminates crucibles; oxygen-free wafers may need nitrogen doping for strength.

title: Cactus: supercritical CO2 cleaning and drying for capacitor pillars
idea: Random stimulus 'cactus' -> thrive with almost no water. Post-etch clean and final dry of capacitor pillars use supercritical CO2 with co-solvents, so there is no liquid-gas meniscus and no capillary collapse, replacing many UPW rinse steps.
why: Cuts fab water use ~30-40% (deserts become siteable) and removes pattern collapse that caps capacitor AR at ~60-75:1, a path to the AR ~115 that fact 1 needs.

title: Magnify build speed: containerized cleanroom fab in 9 months
idea: Factory-build a 20k wafer/month DRAM fab as pre-certified, plug-together cleanroom and utility modules (container-sized, integrated air handling, ultrapure water and gas skids) so tool install starts while the shell is still being bolted together.
why: Shrinks the 3-5 year fab timeline to ~1.5 years, cuts interest during construction, and lets capacity respond within one price cycle.

title: Memory REIT: never own RAM, lease pooled GB-hours
idea: Ideal: memory that is free and always exactly where it is needed. Closest achievable: a memory real-estate trust buys DRAM in bulk at contract prices and leases it by the GB-hour into CXL-pooled racks at clouds and enterprises, reclaiming the 25-50% of server DRAM that sits stranded inside individual servers.
why: Usable supply and cost per bit: ~1.3-1.5x more working bits from the same installed DRAM, and memory capex becomes opex that is financed at REIT cost of capital.

title: PEEK, UHMWPE and quartz fluid handling ending fluoropolymer dependence
idea: Fuse PEEK, UHMWPE and fused-quartz wetted parts with all-metal C-seals and sapphire valve seats, replacing PFA tubing, PTFE valves and FFKM O-rings in non-fluorine chemical and UPW loops. This becomes possible because no HF or fluoride chemistry needs PTFE-grade inertness.
why: Decouples fab construction from the fluoropolymer supply crunch after 3M's PFAS exit, cutting lead time and supply risk for fab buildout.

title: Biologist's apoptosis: sell dies with dead banks as smaller parts
idea: Cells die in a controlled way so the organism survives. Likewise, fuse off the failed banks or subarrays on DRAM dies that miss full spec and ship them as 12 Gb or 8 Gb 'harvested' parts, with a JEDEC capacity descriptor so controllers map only the live banks (GPU binning applied to memory).
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers the ~5-15% of dies scrapped at wafer sort and burn-in, adding supply without a single new wafer.

title: Velcro: R2R nanowire hook film makes demountable reworkable HBM stacks
idea: Random stimulus 'Velcro' -> hook-and-loop that peels and re-fastens. An R2R-grown film of vertical copper nanowire 'hooks' is cold-pressed between stacked die as a demountable interconnect; a die that fails stack test is peeled off and replaced before final underfill.
why: Stack yield up from ~70-80% to >95% by reworking instead of scrapping 8-12 good die, adding ~20% more HBM bits per wafer start.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-hosted as CXL memory via package harvesting
idea: Inverts 'DRAM retires with its server': automated depopulation lines desolder DDR4/DDR5 packages from decommissioned DIMMs, re-characterize each package at speed and temperature, and re-mount them on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller still speaks the old DRAM protocol.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit: reuses silicon whose fab capex is already sunk; at hyperscaler retirement volumes this could add roughly 5-10% of annual server DRAM bits at ~25% of new cost.

title: Fermented masks: bacterial S-layer protein crystals as nano-etch templates
idea: Grow S-layer-bearing bacteria (e.g., Sporosarcina, Deinococcus) in a fermenter, harvest the S-layer proteins, and recrystallize them on wafers as 2D lattices with 10-13 nm periodic pores. Infiltrate them by ALD to make a hard mask for dense hole and pillar arrays: a lithography template brewed in a vat.
why: Litho capital: sub-15 nm periodic patterning for the price of a fermenter, scaling by volume like brewing. Runs in a nanofab plus a bio lab.

title: Zinc-silicon-oxide BEOL gain cells replace IGZO without indium or gallium
idea: Leakage physics depends on bandgap and trap density, not on indium: amorphous Zn-Si-O (~3.5 eV gap, with Si suppressing oxygen vacancies the way Ga does in IGZO) can give 2T0C gain cells with sub-1e-18 A off-current. Build them in the BEOL of any U.S. CMOS foundry, using only Zn, Si and O.
why: Refresh wall and scarce resource: In/Ga-free oxide memory with >100 s retention cuts refresh energy ~1000x and turns every logic fab into a potential memory fab.

title: Slow capacity-tier DRAM with mega-mats to shrink periphery
idea: Po: memory is cheaper because it is slower. Since cells cannot shrink without EUV, periphery shrinks instead: a capacity-tier DRAM uses 2-4x longer bitlines and wordlines per mat, larger pages and fewer sense amplifiers, accepting ~2x tRCD for 150-250 ns CXL-attached memory, with fat DUV capacitors keeping Cs/Cbl workable.
why: Cuts periphery from ~49% to ~25-30% of die, raising bits per wafer ~30-40%; attacks density and cost per bit.

title: Strategic DRAM reserve buys gluts, releases in shortages
idea: Box[Owner=government x Finance=counter-cyclical purchases of graded dies and modules x Storage=N2 vaults x Channel=release auctions]: like a strategic petroleum reserve, the government buys DRAM in downturns, which keeps fabs investing, and auctions it out in spikes like 2026.
why: Cycle damping: stable demand lets fabs add capacity continuously and cuts peak price spikes from ~4x to well under 2x.

title: Minimal-fab half-inch wafers with maskless writing for defense memory
idea: Box[Fab=12.5 mm wafer minimal-fab tool modules x Lithography=maskless direct-write x Medium=oxide gain cell chiplets x Owner=DoD x Finance=program funding x Scale=micro-fab]: build a <$50M micro-line that makes small lots of trusted memory chiplets for weapons and space systems, removing low-volume trusted demand from the commodity market.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: ~1000x lower capex for trusted low-volume memory; frees allocation fights over legacy DRAM.

title: Every byte must be borrowed: off-peak HBM lending over scale-up fabric
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new memory for batch jobs. The cluster scheduler lends idle HBM on lightly loaded inference GPUs at night as remote memory over NVLink-class fabric for training checkpoints and KV spill.
why: Raises HBM utilization from diurnal lows of about 30-40%, which avoids buying extra capacity.

title: Embargo engineer's reballing brigade for e-waste phone LPDDR
idea: Like a Soviet engineer under embargo salvaging chips from Western hardware, automated lines pull LPDDR4X/LPDDR5 packages off scrapped phones and laptops (IR desolder, X-ray inspection, reball). Packages pass 48-hour march and retention screens and are mounted, graded, on CXL Type-3 carrier cards whose controller maps around weak banks.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2B phones a year retire with 4-12 GB each; recovering 10% gives ~1 EB/yr of DRAM-class capacity (a few % of world bit supply) with almost no fab capital.

title: Tire-retread playbook: remanufacture retired server DRAM into CXL pools
idea: Like tire retreading, take DDR4/DDR5 packages from decommissioned hyperscale servers and run a high-temperature retention and row-hammer screen. Reball the good packages and rebuild them onto CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller applies per-device refresh profiles. Sell them as warrantied 'retread' tier-2 capacity, the way remanufactured auto parts are sold.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~15-25% of installed DRAM retires each year still working. Recovering half adds ~5-10% effective bits at <30% of new cost, with zero wafer, EUV or helium intensity.

title: Phone e-waste LPDDR harvest reballed into LPCAMM modules
idea: Fuse an e-waste smartphone/laptop dismantling line with an automated package-rework cell. It hot-air-removes LPDDR4X/5 packages, laser-cleans and reballs them, tests each package on a socketed ATE, and mounts bins of matched speed onto new LPCAMM or soldered edge-device boards.
why: Recovers 4-16 GB per scrapped premium phone (billions in the waste stream) as new-equivalent supply for edge and IoT devices. Cost per bit is about 30-50% of new and needs zero fab capital.

title: Fuse 32 Gb partial-good dies down to JEDEC 24 Gb density
idea: Box[Source=dies with a defective bank group x Transform=e-fuse remap to the standard 24 Gb address map x Integration=standard 24 Gb DDR5 die in 48/96 GB DIMMs x Owner=DRAM maker]: dies with defects beyond row and column repair have the bad quarter fused off and present as a legal JEDEC 24 Gb device.
why: Raises good die per wafer by an estimated 2-5% on new nodes, using the non-binary densities DDR5 already allows.

title: Universality: one universal die with fuse-selected DDR5/LPDDR/HBM-core personality
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: design a single array die whose PHY, burst logic and TSV landing pads support DDR5, LPDDR5X and HBM-core roles, chosen by fuses after wafer sort, so fabs never commit wafers to the wrong product months before demand is known.
why: Product-mix misallocation and inventory whiplash: ~5-10% effective supply gain plus faster response to price spikes.

title: ISO shipping-container standard for bare memory dies
idea: Adapted from the 1956 intermodal container: define a fixed die footprint, hybrid-bond pad grid, power map and self-test port so any fab's DRAM die, of any cell technology, drops into any HBM/CXL stack or package without requalifying the package.
why: Breaks vendor lock-in and lets small fabs and new cell types sell into high-value stacks; widens the supplier pool and shortens qualification (supply, capital intensity).

title: Tungsten recovery skid for WF6 exhaust and chamber shields
idea: Design for a zero-import fab while China holds ~80% of tungsten. A 10-person company builds skid-mounted units that capture unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust as tungstate in alkaline scrubbers and strip W from chamber shields, returning tungsten to precursor makers.
why: Could cut virgin tungsten per wafer 30-60% and hedge the chokepoint.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM slabs from mature DUV nodes
idea: Po: the wafer is the chip. A 25 nm-class DUV DRAM wafer is never diced: on-wafer redundancy, a wafer-level routing mesh and a bonded controller tile expose the whole wafer (~0.5 TB) as one memory slab for rack-level CXL pools, with bad mats mapped out at test.
why: Skips dicing, packaging and module assembly (~15-25% of cost) and lets older DUV fabs supply capacity-tier memory; attacks capital and cost per bit.

title: Lead-free-solder-style coordinated switch to tungsten-free DRAM
idea: Like the RoHS lead-free transition coordinated across the industry, a consortium qualifies molybdenum wordlines and contacts with Cu-Mn barrier-free lines to 10 years at 125 C electromigration and stress-migration, with a sunset date for tungsten.
why: Removes dependence on ~80% China-sourced tungsten while meeting automotive reliability, so the swap happens once for all suppliers.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly writes capacitor lattices with carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
idea: A symmetric diblock copolymer at its free-energy minimum forms hexagonal cylinders at a pitch set by chain length (~20-30 nm), exactly the storage-hole lattice. Guide PS-b-PMMA with a coarse DUV prepattern, harden it by sequential Al2O3 infiltration, and etch storage holes through the alumina mask.
why: Capital and EUV: replaces 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers with spin-coat and bake; defectivity must reach <0.01/cm^2 for full adoption.

title: Substitute TSVs with inductive coupling coils for die stacking
idea: Swap through-silicon vias for on-chip inductor coils patterned in BEOL at <=400 C, giving TSV-free wireless die-to-die links (ThruChip-style) so ordinary thinned DRAM dies can be stacked by any packager.
why: Removes the TSV keep-out area and process (HBM ~3x area per bit) and saves ~10-20% of die area per stacked bit.

title: Substitute product-specific masks with a universal sea-of-cells array mask
idea: Swap per-product mask sets for an industry-shared, standard array mask set covering the memory tiers, and customize each product only through a cheap <=400 C top via and metal layer (structured-ASIC style).
why: Amortizes mask and EUV cost over the whole industry, cutting mask spend per product ~80% and making small-volume memory products viable.

title: Trusted-memory advance market commitment for U.S.-made DRAM
idea: Defense, the extreme price-insensitive user, signs a Warp-Speed-style 10-year take-or-pay commitment for U.S.-fabbed DRAM at a ceiling price, with surplus resold commercially, so a domestic line becomes bankable before it ships.
why: U.S. manufacturability from 1-2% share; turns policy demand into financeable offtake.

title: Eleven-element DRAM process built only from crustal commons
idea: Today's DRAM flow touches ~25 elements, each with its own gas cabinet, precursor chain and qualification. Restrict the whole flow to Si, O, N, H, C, B, P, Al, Ti, Zr and Cu (TiN electrodes, ZrO2/Al2O3 dielectric, poly-Si and TiN local wiring, Al/Cu interconnect), deleting whole classes of precursors and abatement systems.
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity: fewer gas lines, tools and suppliers, and a U.S. fab immune to every listed chokepoint.

title: Arsenal of Democracy retools NAND lines for quasi-volatile 3D NOR
idea: As Detroit retooled car lines for bombers in 1942, NAND makers retool lines now in oversupply to make quasi-volatile 3D NOR. It keeps the 200-layer stack but uses ~2-3 nm direct-tunneling charge-trap cells in a NOR arrangement, aiming for ~100 ns random access, >1e12 cycles and retention of seconds to minutes.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: inherits 3D NAND's ~10-15x areal density over DRAM at NAND-like wafer cost, with rare refresh. Endurance at thin oxide and write latency are the risks.

title: Continuity: government buyer-of-last-resort keeps DRAM fabs at full utilization
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: during downturns a national memory reserve buys known-good die at cost-plus, keeping tools at 100% loading; the stored die (dry-nitrogen cabinets) are released into the market during shortages.
why: Capital efficiency: idle tools waste depreciation; continuous loading plus a strategic buffer flattens price spikes.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve that buys gluts and sells spikes
idea: Po: DRAM is oil. A government reserve buys known-good DRAM dies and modules during price troughs, stores them in nitrogen dry cabinets, and auctions them when contract prices rise more than ~50% year-over-year.
why: Smooths the boom-bust cycle that makes fabs underinvest: trough buying keeps fabs near full utilization and spike releases cap 4x price surges; attacks supply stability and capital risk.

title: Central banker's Strategic DRAM Reserve of nitrogen-stored dies
idea: Treat DRAM like oil: a federal reserve buys known-good DRAM wafers and dies in gluts, when contract prices fall below cash cost, and stores them in dry-nitrogen cabinets where dies keep for over 10 years. It auctions them to U.S. module assemblers when prices pass 2x the trailing average.
why: Supply stability and capital: damps the boom-bust cycle that deters capex; a ~5 EB reserve could cap a 4x spike, keep fabs running full through downturns, and lower every producer's cost of capital.

title: Qimonda lesson: counter-cyclical strategic DRAM wafer reserve
idea: Qimonda went bankrupt in the 2008-09 crash with buried-wordline technology in hand because no one would bridge a 12-month cash trough. Fix: a sovereign reserve buys finished DRAM wafers and known-good dies at a cost-based floor during busts, stores them in nitrogen cabinets (unpackaged wafers keep for years), and releases them at a ceiling price during shortages like 2026.
why: Keeps capacity alive through troughs and flattens spikes: a reserve of ~5% of annual bits could hold a 4x spike nearer 2x, and it prevents capacity destruction that takes $15B and 4 years to rebuild.

title: Open-hardware DRAM tester kits that issue signed grade certificates
idea: Learning from ham-radio networks, a 10-person company sells ~$300 FPGA tester kits with secure elements to e-waste recyclers worldwide. Each run produces a cryptographically signed certificate (pattern suite, retention, speed bin) bound to the module serial, so remote buyers can trust second-hand memory.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in secondary memory markets; signed provenance could unlock millions of modules a year.

title: Magnify throughput 100x: solar-style inline memory lines
idea: Borrow photovoltaic manufacturing (belt-fed inline PECVD, laser scribing, screen-print metallization at ~8,000 wafers/hour per line) to make vertical thin-film transistor-capacitor cells whose critical dimensions are set by film thickness and laser scribe, not lithography.
why: PV processes a wafer for ~$0.2 vs ~$5,000+ for DRAM; even holding ~1/500 of the bits, cost per GB drops ~100x+, accepting low density, big modules and slower first versions.

title: Librarian's catalog: signed lifetime passport on every DIMM
idea: Each module's SPD carries a signed lifetime log written by the host BMC: power-on hours, thermal history, corrected-error counts, row-hammer events. Second-hand buyers can grade modules the way a library tracks a book's condition, and a public registry prices reuse by verified health.
why: Reuse supply: buyers' distrust is the main barrier to secondary DRAM markets; verified provenance could lift reuse from <10% to 40%+ of retired server DRAM.

title: Substitute bonded silicon dies with memory decals from reusable glass carriers
idea: Swap whole-die stacking for building thin oxide-memory tiers on reusable glass carriers at <=400 C, then laser-debonding and laminating them as ~2 um decals onto any target die or wafer, with the carrier reused many times.
why: Decouples memory manufacture from the target wafer's fab; carrier reuse cuts substrate cost and thin decals avoid TSVs.

title: Memory-as-a-lease with mandatory take-back keeps bits circulating
idea: Because DRAM bits do not wear out, transfer of ownership is the real waste mechanism. Manufacturers lease modules by GB-month with RFID-tracked serials and contractual take-back, then redeploy returned modules down a tier ladder (training to inference to enterprise to edge) over ~15 years.
why: Usable supply: triples service life per manufactured bit, multiplying cumulative supply ~2-3x for the same wafer starts.

title: Origami fold-stack: thinned die ribbons folded into TSV-free stacks
idea: Fabricate a ribbon of 4-8 memory dies on a wafer thinned to 30 um, joined by polyimide hinges that carry copper traces. Etch through the silicon between dies and fold the ribbon accordion-style into a stack in which every signal runs through the hinges, as in origami.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): no TSV keep-out and no die-to-die alignment loss. Thinning, hinge patterning and DRIE are nanofab-standard.

title: Insurance pricing rewards fabs that dual-qualify abundant substitutes
idea: Chokepoint disruption is a correlated, quantifiable loss. Business-interruption underwriters price premiums by each fab's banned-element mass dependency and discount fabs that hold pre-qualified abundant substitutes (TiN wordline, Zr-only dielectrics) able to switch within 90 days.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: aligns private capital with resilience; premium savings pay back qualification costs in ~3 years.

title: Preliminary action: pre-permitted state memory megasites with utilities pre-built
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: states pre-permit, pre-grade and pre-plumb fab-ready megasites (substations, reclaimed-water plants, bulk gas, helium recovery, rail) before any tenant signs, so a DRAM maker starts tool install in months, not years.
why: Time and capital: trims 12-18 months from fab schedule; raises U.S. share of DRAM output.

title: Certified remanufactured DRAM: package harvest, reball and warranty standard
idea: Shenzhen rework shops, an extreme informal user, already desolder and reball DRAM from scrap. Formalize it with a UL-style certification covering test protocol, burn-in, traceability and a 3-year warranty, under which retired hyperscaler DIMM packages are harvested, reballed and rebuilt onto new module and CXL PCBs.
why: Tens of millions of DIMMs retire each year; 30% recovery adds several % of global bit supply at ~10-20% of new cost with no fab capex.

title: License-unlocked three-level cell mode raises capacity on installed die
idea: Inverts 'capacity is fixed at manufacture': die ship with dual-mode sense amplifiers that can resolve three charge levels (1.58 bits/cell); customers who accept 1% raw BER buy a firmware license that unlocks ~1.4x net capacity.
why: Bits per wafer: ~40% more usable bits from the same silicon after parity, plus a recurring license revenue line for vendors.

title: Matsushita 1995 Charge-Recycling Bus Revived for Memory I/O
idea: Revive Matsushita's mid-1990s charge-recycling bus, which stacked N bus lanes in series voltage domains so charge drained from one lane powers the next: stack 8 DQ lanes between VDDQ and ground so each swings VDDQ/8 and the same charge is reused eight times.
why: I/O energy per bit drops ~8-10x on DDR/LPDDR interfaces (fact 5: 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5); periphery-only change usable by every DRAM maker.

title: Contract-brewing model: a pure-play DRAM foundry for fabless designers
idea: Craft beer brands contract-brew at big breweries. Create a DRAM foundry with a published cell PDK in which the capacitor and array transistor are fixed and the periphery is open. Fabless firms can then ship specialized DRAM (AI-tuned page sizes, PIM, automotive) without owning fabs, as TSMC enabled for logic.
why: Industry structure: many designers share capacity at higher utilization. Specialized designs that cut overfetch and refresh deliver more usable memory per wafer.

title: Sn: Bismuth-tin low-temperature reballing harvests DRAM from retired servers
idea: An automated line desolders DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards below 170 C with Bi-Sn solder and laser selective reflow, tests each die for retention and hammer threshold, reballs and remounts them as graded modules.
why: Hyperscalers retire exabyte-scale DRAM after 4-6 years; harvesting 30% of it adds several percent to annual supply at near-zero capital.

title: Shipyard block construction of prefabricated cleanroom modules
idea: Like shipyards building hull blocks indoors and joining them, factories prefabricate standardized cleanroom-plus-subfab modules (ducting, piping, tool hookups pre-installed and leak-tested), trucked and bolted together on site.
why: Cuts fab construction from ~36 to ~15 months and capex 10-20%, getting supply online during the shortage instead of after it.

title: Nantero's contamination wall: bolt-on BEOL annex for exotic memory
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM spent more than a decade on adoption because fabs would not let CNTs (or other exotic materials) into their lines. Fix: a small back-end annex beside a logic or DRAM fab receives finished CMOS wafers in sealed pods, deposits and patterns the new memory layers in its own cleanroom, and returns sealed wafers, so the host line never touches the material.
why: Removes the main adoption barrier for new memory materials; an annex costs ~$0.3-1B versus $15B for a fab and lets new memories use existing CMOS capacity.

title: Pastry chef's mille-feuille: 64 tiers of 2D-semiconductor gain cells
idea: A pastry chef folds dough into hundreds of layers. Grow wafer-scale MOCVD MoS2/WSe2 monolayers (0.7 nm thick) and stack 64 transistor tiers separated by 10 nm hBN or oxide. Each tier's storage node is the gate of an ultralow-leakage 2D-channel 2T0C cell, and the whole stack is ~1 um tall. U.S. 2D-material growers become a new supply chain.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density is ~12x/mm^2. The thin tiers keep via etch aspect ratio under 20:1, so per-tier cost is small and wafer cost stays near DRAM's.

title: Federal procurement accepting 1% raw BER opens doors for novel-cell startups
idea: Inverts 'a new cell must match incumbent zero-defect yield on day one': a DARPA/DoD purchase program buys memory specified at 1% raw cell BER plus a post-code UBER target, letting startups ship variable cells such as floating-body or thin-film gain cells years earlier.
why: Supply diversity: creates guaranteed first revenue for new entrants while their yields mature.

title: Tester hours halved: finish DRAM characterization in the deployed server
idea: Self-imposed limit: half the ATE and burn-in hours. Parts ship after a shortened screen; in-DIMM BIST plus post-package repair finish margin and retention characterization during the first week in a server, and the fleet telemetry feeds back to the fab.
why: Test capital and throughput: test/burn-in capacity effectively doubles, removing a back-end bottleneck to bit output.

title: Refurb-tool immersion fab co-owned by used-tool brokers
idea: Combine the secondhand 300mm tool market (ArF immersion scanners, ALD and etch) with a DRAM startup. Tool refurbishers contribute equipment for equity, and the fab runs a 20-25 nm EUV-free 6F² flow with multiple patterning.
why: Capex is about 1/4-1/5 of a leading-edge fab, and it gets running in 18-24 months instead of 3-5 years. It serves the large share of demand that doesn't need 1-gamma density.

title: UCIe DRAM chiplet standard making any fab's die package-fungible
idea: Worse: make every HBM a bespoke co-design locked to one GPU vendor. Flip: define an open DRAM chiplet footprint and protocol over UCIe so a qualified DRAM die from any maker drops into any accelerator package and packagers can mix suppliers per lot.
why: Makes AI memory supply fungible, lets second-tier and U.S. fabs sell into AI packages, and offers lateral chiplets that avoid the TSV tax.

title: CCD memory reborn in idle sensor fabs for weight streaming
idea: CCD shift-register memory (Fairchild, Intel, 1970s) lost to DRAM because of serial access, and CCD sensor fabs are idling as CMOS image sensors won. Serial access is now a feature: AI inference streams weights and KV blocks in fixed order, so many parallel CCD loops built on 0.35-0.18 um CCD lines can stream blocks at full rate with no row decoders and little periphery.
why: Density and periphery: CCD storage is ~4F^2 with almost no periphery (vs ~49% of a DRAM die), giving a cheap streaming tier from stranded fabs; random access stays poor.

title: H2-bake and ozonated-water clean cluster replacing HF dips
idea: Fuse an epi-style in-situ H2 bake (800-850 °C, desorbing native oxide) with ozonated-UPW plus dilute-HCl megasonic cleaning in one vacuum-linked cluster, so wafers never see HF before gate oxide or contact formation.
why: Removes HF, the most common fluorinated fab chemical, along with CaF2 sludge treatment. It simplifies the waste plant and permitting.

title: Hafnium-free AlBN ferroelectric capacitors from abundant elements
idea: Worse: build all nonvolatile capacitor memory on hafnium, a nuclear-zirconium byproduct with few refiners. Flip: use boron-substituted aluminum nitride, a wurtzite ferroelectric, sputtered at back-end temperatures as the nonvolatile capacitor dielectric.
why: Zero refresh from abundant Al, B and N on ubiquitous sputter tools, which helps U.S. manufacturability; high coercive field and endurance are the risks.

title: Zr: Hafnium-free zirconia antiferroelectric with built-in bias stores bits
idea: Put pure antiferroelectric ZrO2 between electrodes of different work function so the built-in field shifts the double hysteresis loop, leaving two stable remanent states at zero volts.
why: Zr is far more abundant than scarce Hf; reuses DRAM ZrO2 ALD tools; antiferroelectric endurance beats ferroelectric.

title: Twin Creeks revived: proton-exfoliated thin DRAM wafers spare crucibles
idea: Twin Creeks' Hyperion proton-implant exfoliation (slicing ~20 um silicon sheets off a thick donor) died in the 2012 solar price crash. Fix: apply it to DRAM by exfoliating many thin device-grade layers from one CZ donor block and bonding each to a cheap recycled or polycrystalline handle wafer, so one crystal ingot yields 10-20x more device wafers.
why: Scarce resources: cuts high-purity quartz crucible and polysilicon use per wafer by roughly 10x, which matters when Spruce Pine supplies >80% of crucible quartz.
